Soon to head outside to tend to the ailing garden of her London home, she is enjoying a rare period of rest after six almost unbroken months of Oedipus on Broadway and then Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National. She keeps, incidentally, the Tony she won for playing Jocasta in Oedipus on a shelf by the computer, “next to its friend, Larry Olivier” – an Olivier awarded for the same role. “You don’t go into a job thinking about awards,” she says, before grinning conspiratorially. “Listen, you don’t say to an Olympian, ‘Oh, is it OK that you didn’t win?’ Yes, you like to win!” Continue reading...

articles.title: The Real Rooneys review – at least Wayne and Coleen’s reality show proves they can laugh at themselves
articles.description: This trip into the celeb couple’s Cheshire mansion is nowhere as real as they’d like you to believe. But their self-deprecation is hard not to enjoy ‘There are two obvious problems here, the first being that the Rooneys’ lives feel like fiction: he was a generational sporting talent, a one-in-a-million player whose success has bought him and Coleen a ridiculous Cheshire mansion with a cinema, indoor pool and adjacent football pitch. To get back to the road you have to drive over a bridge across a lake. As we join them, Coleen is working out how to capitalise on a recent appearance on I’m a Celebrity ... Get Me Out of Here!, while Wayne is plotting an uptick in his media appearances that he hopes will make him a regular on Match of the Day. Technically, the Rooneys exist on our Earth, but – as they both admit, recalling their working-class childhoods in Croxteth, Liverpool – they have left ordinary life behind. Even if we accept that they are to some extent real people, the further problem is that if you want to get to know someone, watching a behind-the-scenes “at home with” reality show is not the way to do it. This is an established format that was initially shaped by the Kardashians and has now evolved to fit the specific needs of retired British sportsmen looking to relaunch themselves as media personalities. By design, the shows are anything but realistic, instead offering a carefully calibrated blend of fantastic luxury that viewers can escape into, and domestic rituals – breakfast, the school run – offered up in a half-hearted attempt to show that really, these famous folk are just like us. Continue reading...

articles.title: Trump’s MAGA Media Plot Backfires After Embarrassing Fail
articles.description: Evan Vucci / REUTERS A right-wing TV station trying to fill the void left by the White House television pool ran into some technical difficulties Wednesday while airing Donald Trump’s comments. Real America’s Voice is partnering with Lindell TV—whose namesake is Mike Lindell, the pro-Trump 2020 election denier and failed Minnesota Senate candidate—to provide its version of the coverage that has been on hold following Trump’s ban of CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House. Several right-wing outlets have picked up where the others left off, including The Daily Wire and The Daily Signal. On Wednesday, when Trump returned to the White House from rolling out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, he walked up to the press pool, which no longer includes television cameras from Fox News, CNN, CBS, ABC or NBC. But as he talked about the South Lawn helipad, one of his pet projects, the feed cut out in parts, leaving him inaudible. Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: Sweet Stash moves its Wonka-esque gummy production to Chicago
articles.description:
More than a century after Wrigley, Brach’s and Mars helped turn Chicago into a candy epicenter, a trio of artists with an unabashed candy obsession brought their gummy candy startup to the shuttered former Jelly Belly plant in suburban North Chicago, ushering in a new era for this storied city of sweets production.

The actor Martin Starr and musicians and identical twins Ezra and Adeev Potash cofounded Sweet Stash last fall with an additive-free gummy with the complex flavor and texture dimension of candies they discovered over years of globe-trekking.

“We are obsessed with candy beyond what’s normal and maybe even healthy,” Ezra said. “We’ve been candy people long before we became candy vendors.”

After months of routinely selling out on Amazon amid swelling requests from retailers for their toothsome, musical note-shaped Jams gummies in flavors like Prickly Pear, Strawbarb and White Peach, the fledgling company moved production from Albion, Nebraska (the twins’ home state) to Ferrara’s 113-year-old Jelly Belly factory in April, effectively quadrupling the previous output in a fraction of the time. The move doesn’t just mean taking on bigger orders and getting onto more indie store shelves while maintaining consistency in a product free from gluten, synthetic dyes and corn syrup. This self-starting trio can also keep making candy limited mostly by their imaginations in a city known for confectionery innovation — a rarity for an industry dominated by profit-seeking conglomerates.

“We’re a small band of creative people going up against billion-dollar companies that make candy by the tank,” Adeev said.

On a hot and sticky recent Thursday, the bespectacled twins and I scooched into a taped-up booth beneath a wood-paneled wall full of bric-a-brac at the 105-year-old Margie’s Candies in Logan Square. The historic shop carries the original Jams, along with the crunchy sugar-coated Rock Jams and tart Sour Jams Sweet Stash that the trio launched this summer.

“If there’s a place we had to be in Chicago, it was here,” Adeev said. “This is an institution for a century. I mean, the pope was just eating Margie’s [three weeks] ago. That’s the reason I love Chicago and the candy world here. It’s a place that loves new things, but that also respects the history.”

Adeev (trumpet) and Ezra (trombone) are musicians first, discovered and mentored by the trumpeter and composer Wynton Marsalis. They’ve released three albums and written scores for the likes of “RuPaul’s Drag Race.” They have also hosted television series for Travel Channel, Bravo and Food Network. As touring musicians, the twins (who divide their time between Los Angeles and Omaha) developed a habit of popping into bodegas after shows in search of candy they’d never tried.

“After years of doing that, we kind of became pseudo-experts on what was available to the public all over the world,” Ezra said. Apparently, candy invention is even in their DNA. In the 1800s their great grandparents owned Wolfberg’s General Store in Wakarusa, Indiana, where they said their great-grandfather, rather presciently, invented the giant jelly bean.

They met Starr in 2022 at a charity event, hosted by celebrities including Jason Sudeikis and Paul Rudd, where the trio became fast friends.

“It was late at night and I think somebody was eating Haribo Goldbears,” Adeev recalled, then Ezra interjected. “We probably said something nerdy, like, ‘I think they’re just the perfect texture, but the flavors are a bit flat.’ And then Martin was probably like, ‘What the hell did I just see?’”

“They didn’t even like candy until they met me,” Starr quipped, reached somewhere in New York on Ezra’s phone.

Known best for his role as the cynical, deadpan Bertram Gilfoyle on HBO’s “Silicon Valley,” Starr has worked as an actor and producer across television and film, including series like the Paramount drama “Tulsa King” (where Sweet Stash makes a handful of cameos), Starz’s “Party Down” and films including “Knocked Up” and “Adventureland.”

Starr’s candy obsession runs deep, too. He recalled as a kid eating gummy bears “to the point where my parents stopped giving me an allowance, because all I spent the money on was candy.”

A few months after they met, Starr invited the “the boys” to his home in L.A. (Starr also lives part-time in Austin, Texas.) Ezra and Adeev remained skeptical of Starr’s candy mania until they glimpsed his cupboards dedicated to candy from around the world, grouped by country and ingredient list, as in, vegan, containing gelatin and gluten-free.

“We’re like, we've actually met our match,” Adeev said.

What’s the ideal amount of chew in a gummy? Can one replicate the physical sensation of peach fuzz in a candy? What should the color green taste like? Such Wonka-esque questions increasingly occupied the minds of the three as their friendship deepened. They wondered why all the confections they love most, featuring layered flavors and invigorating textures, had to be imported from Japan or Australia. They lamented that American candy conglomerates were directing innovation budgets toward injecting sweets with fiber or protein rather than cleaning up their ingredient lists.

“If you want fiber, eat something natural that has fiber it; don’t put in my f------ candy,” Starr said.

They decided to join forces and start a candy company of their own, debuting with an American-style gummy made with high-quality ingredients, a texture that “bites back” and the flavor dimensionality of Japanese and Swedish candies they love. Using their own funds, they recruited candy scientist Tessa Porter, former chief innovation officer of Ferrara, to help develop the additive-free gummies. The designer Ellen Van Dusen, of cult housewares line Dusen Dusen, created the brightly colored packaging. In a nod to the public arts programs that were foundational to the trio’s careers, they donate a percentage of Sweet Stash’s profits to arts education initiatives.

Jams come in six flavors — er, technically 18 if you ask Ezra — which took six months to develop. The three spent hours at a time hashing out each color and accompanying flavor journey. Take Prickly Pear, which starts out tart and pineappley then melony with a tropical, almost floral finish as your teeth slowly work through that springy confection (which by the way isn’t nearly as chewy as these nerds like a gummy). Or Grape, which can, in fact, be green.

“Sorry, but grape doesn't need to be purple and taste like cough syrup,” Adeev said, munching on a crisp Green Grape Rock Jam enrobed in fat sugar crystals. “It could actually taste like the best, juiciest grape you ever had in your life.”

They expected to sell the candy online only until Rudd, who owns a sweets shop in New York’s Hudson Valley, asked to be their first retail customer. Before long, other indie retailers came calling with orders, then reorders. More than 300 specialty retailers nationwide now carry Sweet Stash, including 10 to 15 in Chicago, such as RAYGUN Clothing, Pop/Culture Chicago and the Chicago Athletic Association.

When it became clear Sweet Stash was rapidly outgrowing the Omaha facility, the founders pledged to keep production in the Midwest, which significantly shrunk the pool of plants that could produce a formulation of their standards at scale, they said.

“Production is already allotted to a lot of the big companies; we were lucky to find a place we could grow with in Chicago,” Starr said.

The North Chicago plant churns out 160,000 bags per month, four times the 40,000 bags produced over a months-long run at the Albion plant. With more sophisticated equipment, the team can also maintain precision and consistency over product texture and flavor as it scales and fulfills larger orders.

“It’s still crazy that we have a candy company,” Adeev said. “To see it made in a facility that’s been making one of the most famous candies for 100 years, it’s amazing.”

The move represents a bright spot for a city that has lately seen high-profile confectionery plant closures like Blommers’ and Mars Wrigley’s in addition to Ferrara, which shuttered the Jelly Belly plant in 2024. More sweet news came for Chicago in April, when the National Confectionery Sales Association announced that the city would house the permanent location of the 60,000-square-foot Candy Hall of Fame Experience, at 830 N. Michigan Ave. It is slated to open in 2027.

As far as Sweet Stash is concerned, Chicago remains “Candyland USA,” Ezra said. “Every major candy brand is manufactured here, all the innovation is happening here.”

The latter now includes a trio of candy-obsessed artists, whose enthusiasm seemingly has them leapfrogging confectionery science in the name of whimsy, as they hinted about a potential gummy innovation “so out there that we have to literally wait for the science to catch up,” Ezra said.

Then again, maybe this industry of “billion-dollar Goliaths” needs a little more Willy Wonka energy.

“We’ve been told what we want to create is not possible all the time — as candy even more so,” Adeev said. “For us, making Sweet Stash is like being an actual kid in a candy store. How do you make an everlasting gobstopper? What’s the thing you can’t do?”

Flavor journey


To bite into one of the six Sweet Stash gummy flavors (categorized by tart and rich) is to embark on a texture and flavor journey.

“We’re almost making a caricature of a flavor,” Ezra Potash said. “When you take a bite, it needs to be distilled into the spirit of that flavor while adding others into it that bring out the original.”

The gummy’s al dente chew prolongs said flavor journey, supercharged by the tart-sweet dust coating Sour Jams and fat sugar crystals on the sweet Rock Jams.

Prickly Pear (tart)
Sharp and pineappley to start, the journey turns melony before ending with a tropical, almost floral, finish that croons with pear.

Blue Jazzberry (rich)
The richest of the six and a crowd favorite, this spirulina-dyed blue gummy begins subtly before crescendoing with jammy, complex notes of fresh and cooked raspberry and blackberry.

Strawbarb (rich)
A gentle sweet-sour hum swells into that telltale springtime combo of juicy, brightly floral berry and puckering rhubarb with a crisp finish.

White Peach (rich)
A soft static mimics the lip-tickling fuzz on a peach before the sweet, gently tangy ripe stone fruit notes coat the palate in this clear gummy.

Orange (tart)
The clean, linear burst of citrus peel mingles with marmalade-esque stickiness in this multidimensional take on orange. “This almost didn’t end up in the bag because orange isn’t a flavor profile I gravitate towards — the boys felt similar,” Martin Starr said. “That went through the most rounds of testing. We ended up very happy.”

Green Grape (tart)
Like the snappy burst of crunching into a green grape, this green gummy ricochets gently floral stone fruit and citrus across your tongue, then coasts out with a hum.

articles.title: Review: “Kowalski” at Lookingglass Theatre
articles.description:
There’s a lot of lore underlying the play “Kowalski,” which opened this past weekend at the Lookingglass Theatre.

In 1947, Marlon Brando was a 23-year-old stage actor yet to make his mark. Tennessee Williams, 36 at the time, was following up his first Broadway hit “The Glass Menagerie” with a new play, “A Streetcar Named Desire.”

History tells us that director Elia Kazan gave Brando money to travel to Provincetown, Mass., where Williams was spending the summer, so that the young (and still unknown) actor could read for the part of Stanley Kowalski. Brando pocketed the money and instead hitchhiked with a girlfriend. He arrived three days late but ingratiated himself to the writer by fixing the plumbing and electricity issues plaguing Williams’ bungalow. Then Brando auditioned, got the part, and, some would sincerely say, changed acting forever.

This play by Gregg Ostrin imagines the rest and turns their first meeting into a concentrated clash of personalities — a playwright both cultured and imperious, an actor both unpretentious and manipulative.

“Kowalski”

When: Through October 25th
Where: Lookingglass Theatre (821 N. Michigan Ave.)
Tickets: $37–$97
Info: lookingglasstheatre.org
Running time: 1 hour and 25 minutes with no intermission

Generally amusing in its lighter parts and strained in its more dramatic ones, Ostrin’s work relies on an audience with a decent amount of “Streetcar” knowledge, but not too much. If you don’t know the play or movie, you won’t get some of the humor. But if you know a good amount, you’ll see the fairly gimmicky concept at work before the plot reveals it, since Williams’ masterpiece also centers on a battle between a cultured and imperious Southerner in Blanche DuBois and an unpretentious, manipulative Stanley.

“Kowalski” was initially staged off-Broadway but with different leads. At Lookingglass, Johnny Galecki plays Williams, a clear and purposeful departure from his television roles on “The Big Bang Theory” and “Roseanne.” It’s a highly competent performance, but not an inspired one.

The same is true of Jacob Moskovitz’s (Miles on Amazon Prime’s “Legally Blonde” prequel series “Elle”) turn as Brando. Under Colin Hanlon’s direction, they avoid straight-up impersonations of these famed personalities, but there’s always a sense of performance.

What we ultimately get is an overlayered experience. We’re watching Galecki perform Williams as the character deploys his wit alternately to charm and intimidate a young actor he’s clearly intrigued by. And we’re watching Moskovitz as Brando behaving as Stanley Kowalski.

It reaches peak artifice when the two engage in a power battle over the attentions of Brando’s girlfriend Jo, a role actress Ellie Ricker manages to make likable even though the character is more pawn than person. The other supporting performers here, Alison Cimmet and Reece de Santos, also do solid work with underwritten parts as, respectively, the producer/director Margo Jones and Williams’ boarish (and thus also Stanley-like) boyfriend Pancho.

At just 85 minutes, the play doesn’t overstay its welcome, but I’m puzzled by the stated Broadway aspirations for this piece, no matter how capable the production. First, it’s simply a modest, even standard piece of writing, showing craft but not especially funny and certainly not moving if it’s supposed to be.

It also fails to capture what was genuinely special about both of the artists it depicts, how they changed what theater was and could be by reaching for a more truthful portrayal of humanity, somehow both poetic and raw simultaneously. There is simply nothing either poetic or raw about “Kowalski.”

And finally, I question whether we are still in the age — I wish we were! — when Williams and Brando were figures of such public fascination to make fictional portrayals of them a commercial-level draw.

What we’re primarily left with here is the history, and the nod to artistic greatness.

I appreciate and encourage the production of new plays. But “Kowalski” — as a type of fan fiction — is exactly the type of work that makes me crave the greatness it refers to. It’s not like we’ve been inundated with productions of “Streetcar” – although Paramount Theatre in Aurora staged a very good one in 2024 – or other of Williams’ works. His full-blooded characters remain figures waiting for further discovery and interpretation.

Here’s a call for more of the “real” thing, and less of the lore.
